interviewQuestions.question: You need to speed up a hot path that scans a list of a few hundred items to check membership. Would you switch to a hash set?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It depends on the actual n and what the profiler says, not on Big-O alone. A hash set gives O(1) average membership checks versus O(n) for a linear scan, and past some crossover point that's a real win — but a few hundred items is exactly the range where I'd check before assuming.

First I'd confirm this path is actually significant — profiling it, not guessing, per Performance Mindset & Measurement. If it's genuinely hot, I'd look at what a few hundred sequential integer or pointer comparisons actually cost versus computing a hash and probing a bucket: for small, simple element types, a scan over contiguous memory can be surprisingly close to or faster than hashing, because the array fits in a handful of cache lines and the CPU prefetches it aggressively, while hashing pays a real per-call cost even before touching memory.

At "a few hundred" I'd lean toward benchmarking both rather than assuming — this is squarely in the range where the crossover could go either way depending on element size and how often the set changes (a rebuilt-per-call hash set adds real overhead a persistent one doesn't). If it changes rarely and lookups vastly outnumber rebuilds, hash set is very likely the right call at this size. If it's small, static, and read in a tight loop, I'd measure both before committing.

The one thing I wouldn't do is assume the switch is free money because O(1) beats O(n) — that reasoning has shipped real regressions.

**Testing:** whether you apply Big-O with judgment about actual n and constants, rather than as an automatic rule.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Applied reasoning

interviewQuestions.question: Explain why array-of-structs versus struct-of-arrays can make a huge performance difference for code that has identical Big-O either way.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Big-O only counts operations, not memory access cost — and memory access cost is set by how the hardware fetches data, which is invisible to complexity analysis entirely.

In array-of-structs, each element is a full record (say, x, y, z, and a color field) stored contiguously. If a hot loop only reads `x` across a million elements, each fetch pulls in a full cache line — commonly 64 bytes — that mostly contains y, z, and color the loop never touches. Most of the memory bandwidth pulled into cache is wasted.

Struct-of-arrays stores each field in its own contiguous array. The same loop reading `x` now fetches cache lines that are entirely `x` values — every byte pulled in gets used, so the same number of elements requires far fewer cache-line fetches, often several times fewer.

This is why the technique shows up in game engines (particle systems iterating over one field across thousands of entities), scientific computing, and is effectively baked into columnar databases at the storage-format level, since analytical queries typically touch a handful of columns across huge numbers of rows — row-oriented storage would be the AoS-equivalent mistake at the database layer.

The general lesson: when a hot loop touches a small subset of fields across a large collection, laying memory out by field rather than by record is a constant-factor win invisible to any complexity analysis.

**Testing:** whether you understand cache-line mechanics well enough to explain a real, measurable effect that Big-O simply cannot capture.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: A junior engineer proposes replacing a linked-list-based queue with an array-based one purely for performance, with no algorithmic change. Is that a legitimate optimization?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes, and it's a genuinely common and effective one — it's a memory-layout change, not an algorithmic one, and it's exactly the kind of win that's invisible to Big-O but very visible on real hardware.

A linked list scatters its nodes across the heap wherever the allocator happened to place them. Traversing it means following a pointer to an essentially random address each time, which the CPU's prefetcher can't predict, so nearly every node access is a cache miss — roughly 100x the cost of an L1 cache hit. An array-backed queue (a ring buffer, typically) stores elements contiguously, so sequential access lets the prefetcher pull ahead and keep the CPU fed without waiting on memory.

Both are O(n) to traverse and O(1) for the queue operations that matter (enqueue/dequeue at the ends, if implemented as a ring buffer) — the complexity class is identical. The difference is purely how the hardware experiences the access pattern, and in practice it's large enough that array-backed queues are the default choice in performance-sensitive systems (message queue implementations, game engines, low-latency trading systems) specifically for this reason.

The one caveat I'd flag: an array-based queue needs to handle growth (resizing, which linked lists avoid) and doesn't support O(1) removal from the middle the way a list can — so it's the right default for FIFO/LIFO access, not a universal replacement.

**Testing:** whether you can identify a legitimate, well-known optimization and articulate the mechanism, rather than dismissing it as premature because it doesn't change the algorithm.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You inherited a hot path that allocates a new object on every single invocation, called tens of thousands of times per second. How would you approach fixing it, and what would make you hesitate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First I'd confirm this path is actually a measured bottleneck — if a profiler shows allocation or GC time is a meaningful fraction of the request budget, it's worth fixing; if it's 1% of total time, this is premature optimization regardless of how wasteful it looks in code review.

Assuming it's confirmed hot, my first move is the simplest fix: can the allocation be avoided entirely by reusing a buffer across calls — a single pre-allocated object that gets cleared and overwritten rather than freshly allocated? That's lower-risk than pooling because there's no checkout/return protocol to get wrong.

If the object genuinely needs to be handed out to multiple concurrent callers (so a single shared buffer won't work), I'd reach for an explicit pool — a fixed set of reusable objects checked out and returned. Here's where I'd hesitate: pooling adds real complexity — a whole bug class around using an object after it's been returned to the pool, plus a fixed memory footprint held even when the path is idle. I'd want to see the profiler's evidence that allocation/GC is the actual cost before taking on that complexity, and I'd want tests specifically covering the checkout/return lifecycle, because that's where pooling bugs live.

I'd also check whether the underlying language's escape analysis could avoid the heap allocation entirely (stack-allocating short-lived objects) before reaching for a hand-rolled pool — sometimes the simpler fix is restructuring the code so the object never escapes to the heap in the first place.

**Testing:** whether you weigh the real complexity cost of pooling against measured benefit, rather than reaching for it reflexively.
